p: When I was a boy, a third of all children in England died before they were five years old, and no one, not the most learned physician in London, knew why people caught fevers. The commonest opinion held that disease arose from miasma, a poisonous vapour rising from filth, swamps and decaying matter, which is why the Italians called one fever mal aria, meaning bad air. There was enough truth in it to be dangerous: filth does breed disease, and the sanitary reformers, who cleaned the streets and drained the towns for fear of miasma, saved many thousands of lives for the wrong reason. But the true cause was something no one had seen.

Some had seen it. In the sixteen-seventies, a Dutch draper named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, of Delft, who made the finest microscopes of his age, saw in drops of water and in the scrapings of his own teeth multitudes of tiny living things, which he called little animals, and described in letters to the Royal Society. No one connected them with disease.

In seventeen ninety-six, Dr Edward Jenner, a country doctor of Berkeley in Gloucestershire, not far from here, tested a belief of the milkmaids that those who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, never caught smallpox. He took matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of a dairymaid named Sarah Nelmes and scratched it into the arm of a boy named James Phipps, and later exposed the boy to smallpox. The boy did not take it. From the Latin vacca, meaning a cow, the method came to be called vaccination. It spread across the world, and the Encyclopaedia tells me that, after a great campaign by the nations of the world, smallpox, which had killed perhaps three hundred million people in the twentieth century alone, was declared entirely extinct in nineteen-eighty. It is the only human disease ever to have been destroyed. Jenner did not know why his method worked. He only knew that it did.

In eighteen forty-seven, Dr Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian physician at the great maternity hospital in Vienna, noticed that the women delivered by the doctors and students died of childbed fever far more often than those delivered by the midwives. The doctors came straight from dissecting corpses. He made them wash their hands in a solution of chlorinated lime, and the deaths fell dramatically. His colleagues, offended at the suggestion that gentlemen's hands could be unclean, rejected him, and he died, in eighteen sixty-five, in an asylum. And in eighteen fifty-four, Dr John Snow, of London, traced an outbreak of cholera in Soho to a single public pump in Broad Street, and persuaded the parish to remove its handle. The outbreak was already declining, and the Board of Health rejected his explanation that cholera was carried in water. He was right.

The proof came from France, in my own middle age, and from a chemist rather than a physician. Louis Pasteur, studying why wine and beer go sour, showed in the eighteen-sixties that fermentation and putrefaction are caused by living micro-organisms, and that these do not arise spontaneously from matter, as many believed, but come from other such organisms carried in the air. Broth boiled and sealed in a flask with a long curved neck, which admits air but not dust, remained clear for ever. If micro-organisms cause putrefaction, might they not cause disease? Pasteur went on to study the diseases of silkworms and, in the years to come, the Encyclopaedia tells me, of sheep and chickens and men, and to make vaccines against anthrax and rabies.

Mr Joseph Lister, now professor of surgery at Edinburgh, reading Pasteur, reasoned that the infections that killed so many of his patients after operations, often half of those whose limbs were amputated, were caused by germs entering the wounds. From eighteen sixty-seven he began to clean wounds, instruments and dressings with carbolic acid, and the deaths after his operations fell remarkably. Many of his colleagues still mock him. They will not mock him long.

The Encyclopaedia tells me that it will be a German country doctor, Robert Koch, who next year will show that a particular bacterium causes anthrax, and in eighteen eighty-two will discover the bacterium of consumption, the disease which has killed more of my friends than any other, and lay down rules by which it can be proved that a particular germ causes a particular disease. In the following twenty years, the germs of cholera, typhoid, diphtheria, plague, leprosy and many more will be identified. The germ theory of disease will be established beyond question.

Knowing the enemy is not the same as defeating it. For that, the Encyclopaedia says, mankind waited until the twentieth century. In September nineteen twenty-eight, a Scottish bacteriologist at Saint Mary's Hospital in London, Alexander Fleming, returning from a holiday, noticed that a dish of bacteria he had left on his bench had been contaminated by a mould, and that around the mould the bacteria had died. He named the substance the mould produced penicillin, after the Latin name of the mould. He could not purify it in useful quantities, and little came of it for a decade. Then, at Oxford, in the first years of the Second World War, a team led by an Australian, Howard Florey, and a German refugee, Ernst Chain, with Norman Heatley, who improvised apparatus from milk churns, bedpans and bathtubs, purified penicillin and showed that it could cure infections in mice and then in men. The first patient, a policeman named Albert Alexander, began to recover, and then died when the supply ran out. Under the pressure of war, American factories learned to make it in vast quantities, and by the invasion of France in nineteen forty-four there was enough for every wounded Allied soldier.

Penicillin was the first of the antibiotics, a word meaning against life, that is, against the life of the bacteria. With them, and with vaccines against one disease after another, the Encyclopaedia records that the expectation of life in the richer nations rose from about forty years in my own day to about eighty. Diseases that killed my friends, consumption, scarlet fever, diphtheria, septic wounds, became curable or preventable.

Fleming himself warned, in nineteen forty-five, that bacteria exposed to too little of the drug would learn to resist it. The Encyclopaedia tells me that his warning has come true, and that the physicians of the future are anxious about germs which no antibiotic will kill. The war against the invisible enemies, it seems, is never finally won. But it has given my great-grandchildren, if I had any, twice the years that I was promised.
